stimulus.text:
“Grant that their minds are by nature equal, yet who shall wonder at the apparent superiority, if indeed custom becomes second nature; nay if it taketh place of nature, and that it doth the experience of each day will evince. . . . May we not trace its source in the difference of education, and in the difference of the objects to which the attention of the two sexes is directed?”
— Judith Sargent Murray, “On the Equality of the Sexes,” Massachusetts Magazine, March–April 1790 (written 1779; abridged)
stimulus.source_note: Judith Sargent Murray, “On the Equality of the Sexes,” Massachusetts Magazine, March-April 1790. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus viewed before writing — Judith Sargent Murray, “On the Equality of the Sexes” (1790), public domain.

books.section: Topic 3.6 The Influence of Revolutionary Ideals, B. Evolving Ideas on Gender

primary_sources: Judith Sargent Murray, “On the Equality of the Sexes” (1790)

stem: Murray's argument is that women's apparent inferiority comes from

options.text: A natural weakness of the female mind that no schooling can fix
options.misconception: Murray argues the opposite: minds are “by nature equal,” and the gap comes from custom and schooling, not nature.

options.text: A lack of interest among women in serious study
options.misconception: Murray never blames women's interest; she blames the education offered them, which directs their attention elsewhere.

options.text: Custom and unequal education, not from any natural difference
Laws that barred women from owning property in Massachusetts
options.misconception: Property law never appears in the passage; Murray's cause is custom and the difference of education.

rationales.C: Murray grants that minds are “by nature equal” and traces the gap to custom — “second nature” — and to the different education given to each sex.
rationales.A: Nature is exactly what she rules out; her first line grants that minds are equal by nature.
rationales.B: Interest is not her cause; the cause is what education directs each sex to attend to.
rationales.D: Property law is not her subject; the passage argues about minds, custom, and education.
rationales.general:
1. Read her grant. “Their minds are by nature equal” — nature is ruled out as the cause.
2. Read her cause. Custom becomes “second nature,” and education differs by sex.
3. Rule out the rest. No law, no lack of interest, and no natural weakness appears in the passage.
Remember: when an author names the cause, take it — do not import a different cause from outside the passage.
